newsitem.title: FINLAND: Doubts persist amid Finnish forestry rally.
newsitem.headline: Doubts persist amid Finnish forestry rally.

text.p: A recent surge in Finnish forestry shares could hold for a couple of months but does not yet signal a sustainable upturn as price prospects for pulp and paper are still dim, analysts said on Tuesday.
"We think this is not yet the turnaround of a permanent trend...(though) it could last for a month or two supported by the strong dollar," said Anna-Maija Pirskanen at Merita Bank.
The Helsinki Stock Exchange's forestry share sub-index was nearly two percent ahead in midsession on Tuesday.
Since late last week, the subindex has risen over seven percent, just behind its Stockholm counterpart which started climbing last Thursday and has added over 11 percent.
Both subindices have sharply underperformed their bourses' general indices since late September.
Pirskanen pointed to the strong dollar and Finnish forestry shares' recently lagging prices on a rising market as the likely root of the rise.
"The boom we see now is a short-term boom. It has no fundamentals in paper and pulp prices," said Niels Leth of Den Danske Bank in Copenhagen.
But he said gains in Finnish forestry shares looked more tenable than that of their Swedish counterparts.

"There is more momentum in the Finnish forestry share price increase because they are lower priced," he said. "Swedish shares are now priced at a premium ... while Finnish forestry shares are below market," Leth said.

A research note published by Den Danske in late November showed Swedish companies priced around 10-13 and 9-10 times 1997 and 1998 earnings, with the Finnish companies covered by the bank nearer 8-9 and six times respectively.

A London analyst, who spoke anonymously, said the upswing in Finnish forestry stocks was at least partly a recovery from recent weakness and that the shares could still go higher, but that paper and pulp pricing pitfalls lay ahead.
"There is still a lot of bad news to come in pulp and paper prices ... as inventories build up over the winter," he said.

Analysts cited a discount for Asian pulp prices, fuelling increasing imports, as risking a squeeze in the market price for Northern Bleached Softwood Kraft (NBSK) to around $500/tonne from $560 this week, according to the Finnish Options Exchange.
Nonetheless, optimists do remain with some analysts saying recent economic indicators, especially from Germany, show Europe's economy is starting to find a firmer footing.
"I don't think this can be a bubble," said Paivi Palomaki, analyst at Aktia Bank in Helsinki. "The recovery of the economic cycle has been the basis for this rise."
Even if forestry shares recoil from their fast rise of the past few days, she said the overall trend would be upward as uncertainties about the economy evaporate.
Others stressed the trading factor behind the gains, underlining the fact Finnish forestries have underperformed the market as a whole.
"One reason for this is that forestry shares look underpriced as the whole market has risen," said Jukka Huuskonen of Arctos Securities. "They have clearly underperformed this year."
